CS 301 · Meeting 14 · Act 3

The Axes of a Cloud

Principal axes describe the spread of centred data. Covariance eigenvalues give the variance along each axis and determine rank and condition number.

Mean ratings from two groups of users

  • The 610 people split at random in two halves; a movie's x and y: its mean rating from each half
  • 1,297 points; r = 0.78: the cloud leans on the diagonal
Notes. Split the people at random into two halves and give every movie two numbers: its mean rating from one half and from the other. The movies become a cloud of 1,297 points, and the cloud leans on the diagonal, because the two halves largely agree: r is 0.78. The two arrows are what this act finds: the direction along which the cloud is most spread out, and the direction at a right angle to it.

Projections onto a direction

pi=(xi−μ)·u,‖u‖=1p=XcuVar(p)=1n∑ipi2
  • The dot product gives a signed coordinate along the line
  • np.var(Xc @ u): all 1,297 projections in one product, then their variance
Notes. Centre the cloud by subtracting its mean point. The scalar projection onto a unit direction u is the dot product of the centred point with u. Multiplying that scalar by u gives the projected point in centred coordinates. All the projections at once are the product Xc times u, and their variance says how spread out the cloud is along u. Turn the line: along the horizontal the variance is small, at twenty degrees larger, and at the first axis largest. The page turns the line with a slider; the picture shows three stops.

The first principal axis

axis 1: direction (-0.71, -0.70), singular value 22.4, variance of the projections 0.386
axis 2: direction (0.70, -0.71), singular value 7.9, variance of the projections 0.048
the ratio of the two axes: 2.84
for comparison, the variance of the projections on (1, 0), the horizontal axis: 0.219
Correct: the variance along the diagonal is 0.386, against 0.386 along axis 1, which the svd found at (-0.711, -0.703): the diagonal is almost, not exactly, the best direction.
  • The first principal axis: the direction u with the largest variance of the projections
  • Here u ≈ ±(0.71, 0.70); either sign describes the same axis
Notes. The first principal axis is the direction along which the variance of the projections is largest. For this cloud it is 0.71, 0.70, almost the diagonal: along it, both halves rate a movie high or both rate it low. The notebook's check compares the variance along the exact diagonal with the variance along the axis the computation found: the computed axis gives a slightly larger variance than the exact diagonal. The second axis is at a right angle, where the two halves disagree.

Two axes, an ellipse

  • The second axis: perpendicular to the first; the smallest variance
  • Drawn to two standard deviations: 1.24 and 0.44 stars
  • The singular value of an axis: the length of the vector of all the projections, σ = std · √n
Notes. The second axis passes through the mean, perpendicular to the first; along it the projections have the smallest variance. Each axis is drawn to two standard deviations of the projections on it, 1.24 and 0.44 stars, and the dashed ellipse has those semi-axes. The singular value of an axis is the length of the whole vector of projections, which is the standard deviation times the square root of n: 22.4 and 7.9 here. The ratio of the two is the same whichever way they are measured.

Axes from the covariance matrix

Cov=1nXcTXc,Covv=λv,λk=σk2nκ(Xc)=σ1σ2,κ(Cov)=λ1λ2=κ(Xc)2
the covariance matrix Xc.T @ Xc / n:
[[0.219 0.169]
 [0.169 0.215]]
its eigenvalues: 0.386 and 0.048; its eigenvectors: (-0.71, -0.70) and (+0.70, -0.71)
the singular values of Xc, from np.linalg.svd: 22.37 and 7.88; squared and divided by n: 0.386 and 0.048
condition number of Xc: 2.84 = np.linalg.cond(Xc) = 2.84; of the covariance matrix: 8.05, its square
  • The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix are the axes; its eigenvalues the variances along them
  • np.linalg.eigh(Xc.T @ Xc / n); np.linalg.svd(Xc) gives the same axes and the σ
Notes. Put the centred points in the rows of a matrix: n rows, two columns. Its covariance matrix is X transposed times X over n, the product of Act 1 without the standardization. Its eigenvectors are the two axes and its eigenvalues are the variances along them: 0.386 and 0.048, the squared singular values over n. The condition number of the data matrix is the ratio of its singular values, 2.8, as np.linalg.cond reports; the condition number of the covariance matrix is the ratio of its eigenvalues, 8.1, the square. The notebook calls np.linalg.svd for the axes; eigh of the covariance matrix gives the same, up to the arbitrary sign of each axis. Meeting 15 explains the SVD factorization.

Compressing the second coordinate

  • Multiply the coordinate along axis 2 by a factor; nothing is re-centred or re-standardized
  • κ(Xc), the ratio of singular values, grows; at factor 0 the rank drops from 2 to 1
  • The columns x and y as two vectors: the angle whose cosine is r closes
Notes. The slider of the page: multiply every point's coordinate along axis 2 by a factor between one and zero, with the coordinate along axis 1 and the mean left as they are, and nothing re-standardized. The second axis shrinks and the ratio of the axes, the condition number, climbs: 2.8, 14, 142. Below, the two centred columns as two vectors in the plane they span, at the angle whose cosine is r: as the cloud flattens the columns turn toward each other. Two nearly parallel columns give a nearly singular matrix, the picture of the nearly parallel lines of meeting 13 read for columns instead of rows. At zero, y is a multiple of x and the rank drops from two to one.

Principal axes of the genre data

C=1nZTZ,Cvk=λkvk,k=1,…,19
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(C)      # symmetric; increasing order
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eigenvalues[::-1], eigenvectors[:, ::-1]  # largest first
share = eigenvalues / eigenvalues.sum()            # the variance share of each axis
  • Each movie: 19 standardized genre coordinates; the cloud has 19 axes
  • The axes: the eigenvectors of the 19 × 19 correlation matrix, the principal components
  • The eigenvalues: the variances along them. Finding them is PCA
Notes. The same question for the genre matrix: each movie is a point with 19 coordinates, its standardized genre columns, and the cloud has 19 axes. They are the eigenvectors of the 19 by 19 correlation matrix of Act 1, each a list of 19 weights, one for each genre; the eigenvalues are the variances along them. The axes are the principal components of the data and finding them is principal component analysis. np.linalg.eigh does it for a symmetric matrix, in increasing order, so the notebook reverses.

The genres on the first two components

component 1: negative weights ['Thriller', 'Crime', 'Action', 'Mystery'], positive weights ['Children', 'Animation', 'Musical', 'Comedy']
component 2: negative weights ['Drama', 'Romance', 'Comedy', 'Crime'], positive weights ['Adventure', 'Action', 'Sci-Fi', 'IMAX']
components needed for half of the variance: 6 of 19; for 90%: 15
Notes. The 19 genres by their weights in the first two components, 13 and 12 percent of the variance. Component 1 separates Thriller, Crime, Action and Mystery from Children, Animation, Musical and Comedy: dark and tense against family and musical, in one reading; the notebook asks the students for theirs. Component 2 separates Drama and Romance from Adventure, Action and Sci-Fi. Musical sits far out although only 55 movies have it: standardizing a column with few ones gives those few movies a large weight. On the right, the spectrum: no component dominates; 15 of 19 are needed for 90 percent of the variance.

Rank and condition number

the largest eigenvalue 2.558, the smallest 0.349, their ratio 7.33
the square root of the ratio 2.707; np.linalg.cond(Z) = 2.707
the rank of Z: 19 of 19 columns
  • The rank of Z: the number of nonzero eigenvalues: 19, every direction has spread
  • κ(C) = λmax / λmin = 7.3; κ(Z) = √7.3 = 2.7 = np.linalg.cond(Z)
  • A zero eigenvalue: a direction with no spread; a column that is a combination of the others
Notes. Three things are read from the 19 eigenvalues, the spectrum. The number of nonzero eigenvalues is the rank of Z: 19, the data is spread along every direction. The ratio of the largest to the smallest is the condition number of the correlation matrix, 7.3, and its square root, 2.7, is the condition number of Z, the number np.linalg.cond computes, as for the two-column cloud. And a zero eigenvalue would mean a direction with no spread at all: a column that is a combination of the other columns. The next slide makes one.

A dependent column: Family = Animation + Children

the smallest of the 20 eigenvalues: 1.7e-15, zero up to round-off; the numerical rank of Z20: 19 of 20 columns
with noise of standard deviation 0.05 on Family: the smallest eigenvalue 0.0058, the ratio 569, np.linalg.cond(Z20n) = 23.9
  • A column that is the sum of two others: one eigenvalue 0 up to round-off; rank 19 of 20; exact κ infinite
  • With noise: nearly a sum; the eigenvalue 0.006, κ(C) ≈ 570, κ(Z) = 24
Notes. Add a twentieth column, Family, the sum of the Animation and Children columns. The twentieth eigenvalue is zero up to round-off, about ten to the minus sixteen; the rank is 19 of 20; the exact condition number is infinite, and a huge finite result from np.linalg.cond reflects floating-point error in a matrix that is exactly rank deficient. With a little noise on that column it is no longer an exact sum: the eigenvalue is 0.006, the ratio about 570, the condition number of the data 24. The notebook asks the students to predict the zero before running the cell, and the page has the button and the noise slider; students can use the example from class to explain their prediction in the notebook.

Variance captured by the principal axes

  • Axes needed for 90% of the variance: 240 of 610 for the ratings, 190 of 300 for the words, 15 of 19 for the genres
  • All three need many axes to retain 90% of the variance
  • The Family example illustrates exact rank deficiency
Notes. The same spectrum question for three matrices of the course: the movies as points with 610 user-centred coordinates, the 50,000 words with 300 coordinates, the movies with 19 genre coordinates. How many axes hold 90 percent of the variance: 240 of 610, 190 of 300, 15 of 19. These examples need many axes to retain 90 percent of their variance. The dependent Family column illustrates exact rank deficiency. The words are the instructor's practical question: their 300 dimensions are nearly uncorrelated on average, the centred word matrix has full column rank and condition number about 34, and copying a dimension does to it what Family did to the genres.

Matrix calculations for exploring data

the questionthe matrixcalculationread as
How do the features relate?Z: columns standardizedZ.T @ Z / ncorrelations
How similar are two columns?U: unit-length columnsU.T @ Ucolumn cosines
How similar are two rows?U: unit-length rowsU @ U.Trow cosines
Where is the cloud spread?Xc: columns centredeigh(Xc.T @ Xc / n)axes, variances, rank, κ
  • Normalize the vectors being compared. PCA also requires an eigendecomposition.
Notes. For correlations, standardize the columns and form Z.T @ Z / n. For cosine similarity, normalize the vectors being compared: columns for U.T @ U, rows for U @ U.T. For PCA, centre the point coordinates, form the covariance matrix, and compute its eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Its nonzero eigenvalues count the rank of the centred data. With full column rank, the eigenvalue ratio is the covariance condition number; its square root is the data matrix condition number. Filling missing ratings and choosing a normalization affect these results.
